newsitem.title: INDIA: India sets stringent norms for export refineries.
newsitem.headline: India sets stringent norms for export refineries.

text.p: India's Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) has fixed stringent norms for approving export-oriented refineries, an Industry Ministry document obtained by Reuters on Monday said.
To ensure speedy implementation of proposals, the FIPB will approve the projects only after the promoters achieve specified physical targets within a year of "in-principle approval".
The FIPB has said that future clearance for the refineries be done in two stages.
"In the first stage, an in-principle approval -- valid for one year -- will be given stipulating the milestones to be reached within that period.
"On satisfactory fulfilment of the conditions at the end of the year, FIPB will convert the in-principle approval to a formal one," the document said.
The in-principle approval will lapse if the milestones are not achieved by the year-end, it said.

The milestones to be achieved by the promoters include acquisition of land; mobilisation of up to 15 percent equity from financial institutions; evidence of efforts to secure institutional loans; and tie-ups for export of refined products.

Oil industry officials said the decision was a fallout of poor progress at the export-oriented refineries approved by the FIPB so far. These refineries, some of which were approved as far back as 1993, are yet to get off the ground.
The FIPB has so far granted letters of intent to seven private companies for a refinery capacity addition of 29.3 million tonnes per annum.

Included in the seven are a five million tonne refinery promoted jointly by Mobil Pacific Singapore Limited and India's Pennar Group; a five million tonne refinery of International Petroleum SA (BVI) of Switzerland; a three million tonne refinery promoted by Aban Lloyd Chiles Offshore and India Offshore Inc of the United States; and a 4.8 million tonne refinery from Petro Dyne Inc of the U.S.
The FIPB also decided not to relax the norm on value additions by these refineries, which are obliged to achieve a minimum export earnings of 20 percent over-and-above the value of imports.

"These units should adhere to the prescribed value addition norms without which the domestic economy will have little to gain considering that the employment potential of such refineries is insignificant and these units access scarce domestic capital," the document said.
"Further, such refineries may impose demands on coastal land and infrastructural facilities which may aggravate the already difficult situation at some ports."
The value addition norm would not apply to units which are fully funded through foreign capital and which do not propose to sell 25 percent of their output in the domestic tariff area.
Under India's Export-Import Policy, export-oriented units are allowed to sell up to 25 percent of the output value in the domestic market.
